title: Vishnu Sahasranamam Lyrics with Meaning: Verses 5-6
desc: Vishnu Sahasranamam verses 5 to 6 in Sanskrit with a simple English meaning and how to chant them: 'स्वयम्भूः शम्भुर् आदित्यः पुष्कराक्षो महास्वनः'.
alt: Lord Vishnu, Vishnu Sahasranamam verses 5 to 6 with meaning
caption: Vishnu Sahasranamam, verses 5 to 6.
intro: **Vishnu Sahasranamam** is the thousand names of Lord Vishnu, taught by Bhishma to Yudhishthira in the Mahabharata. This post gives **verses 5 to 6** with the Sanskrit text and a plain English meaning, so you can chant with understanding.
takeaways: The verses here open with **स्वयम्भूः शम्भुर् आदित्यः पुष्कराक्षो महास्वनः**.
Read the Sanskrit slowly, then the meaning, then chant once more.
Thursday and Ekadashi are the days most families keep for Vishnu Sahasranamam.
A short daily portion is better than a rushed full reading.

p: Read the lines aloud, one breath for each half of a verse:
**स्वयम्भूः शम्भुर् आदित्यः पुष्कराक्षो महास्वनः । अनादिनिधनो धाता विधाता धातुर् उत्तमः ॥** **अप्रमेयो हृषीकेशः पद्मनाभोऽमरप्रभुः । विश्वकर्मा मनुस्त्वष्टा स्थविष्ठः स्थविरो ध्रुवः ॥**

Self-born, the giver of happiness, shining like the Sun, is he. Lotus-like eyes and a deep, majestic sound belong to that Supreme Self. He has no beginning and no end, and he is the ordainer who upholds all. No one can measure him, and he is the master of the senses. Padmanabha, with the lotus in his navel, the Lord even of the gods, is that God of gods. The architect of the universe, ever steady, is he.
Light a lamp, sit facing east and chant these verses once, then read the meaning silently. Many families take two verses a day and finish the full text in a little under two months.
The names do not need a long ritual. What matters is steady practice, a clear pronunciation and a calm mind.

ul: Thursdays, the day of Vishnu and the planet Jupiter.
Early morning after a bath, or in the evening at the lamp.

faq.q: What do Vishnu Sahasranamam verses 5 to 6 mean?
faq.a: Self-born, the giver of happiness, shining like the Sun, is he. Lotus-like eyes and a deep, majestic sound belong to that Supreme Self. He has no beginning and no end, and he is the ordainer who upholds all. No one can measure him, and he is the master of the senses. Padmanabha, with the lotus in his navel, the Lord even of the gods, is that God of gods. The architect of the universe, ever steady, is he.
**Bhishma** taught it to Yudhishthira on the field of Kurukshetra, as told in the Anushasana Parva of the Mahabharata.

faq.q: Can I chant a few verses a day instead of the whole text?
faq.a: Yes. A small daily portion with the meaning understood is a common and accepted way to learn it.

note: The Sanskrit is the traditional text. The English is our own plain rendering of the meaning.
